note:
The author identifies himself only as “the elder” and the addressee only as “the elect lady.” These terms are appropriate for a relationship of mutual love and respect in which the author has had pastoral responsibility for the addressee. John’s concern for her depends on the truth all Christians share and is an example of the love that binds all Christians together. It is also possible that the “elect lady” refers to the local church to which John writes and “her children” to the members of the church (see Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes).

**1 The elder.** There is no real difficulty with an apostle (John) identifying himself as an elder, since the responsibilities of an apostle toward each individual congregation included the responsibilities of an elder (1 Pet. 5:1–4).

**the elect lady.** Some consider this expression and the similar expression in v. 13 as a metaphor for a church, though such an expression is otherwise unknown in Scripture. However, it is true that a church is referred to as “she” in 1 Pet. 5:13, and the church in Corinth is compared to Eve, who is said to be betrothed to one husband (2 Cor. 11:2, 3); likewise, the church universal is said to be a “bride” in Rev. 19:7, a “woman” in Rev. 12:1–6, and “a bride adorned for her husband” in Rev. 21:2 (cf. Rev. 21:9). Israel herself was viewed as a bride in the OT (Is. 62:5). These examples provide conceptual precedent for the elect lady’s representing a church. In any case, whether the lady in view is a church or an individual, she is “elect” because of God’s sovereign and gracious choice (John 10:15, 29; 15:16, 19; 17:6; Rom. 9:1–29; 1 Cor. 1:27–31).

**love in truth ... who know the truth.** John first says that he loves the lady (church) and her children (members) _truly_(“love in truth”); then he adds the definite article to speak of “the truth”—which certainly includes gospel doctrine (abiding in the teaching of Christ; v. 9) but also takes on more personal connotations in v. 2.

verse_quote: the truth that abides in us ... will be with us forever.
note: In John’s gospel, Jesus describes Himself as “the truth” (John 14:6) and promises to abide in and be with those who follow Him (15:5; 14:18, 23). He also promises that the Spirit of truth will be in believers and “with you forever” (14:16, 17). In 1 John 1:2, “eternal life” is a name for Christ, who was with the Father and became manifest among us; thus, it appears that “the truth” here represents the constant presence of the Son of God with believers through His Spirit.

As the apostle Paul does, John begins his greeting with mention of the rich Christian blessings of grace and peace (Gal. 1:3 note), but adds “mercy.” The source of this blessed “grace, mercy, and peace” is none other than God Himself, who is truth (John 14:6; 1 John 5:6) and love (1 John 4:8).

The elder and the lady share the joy of seeing members of her household continue to be faithful to the truth. The mark of Christian faithfulness is love for one another, the central command given to Christians by Jesus Himself (John 13:34). That love is defined by all the commands Christ gave His followers.

False teachers had been troubling some of the Christian communities by attacking the central truth of the gospel—that Jesus is the Anointed One, the eternal Son of God who took on human nature to accomplish salvation (1 John 2:22; 4:2, 3). To reject this truth is to reject all hope of reconciliation with God, while to receive it is to receive God Himself. John warns the lady and her household (church) that the work of false teachers threatens their spiritual progress (v. 9 note) and even their hope of eternal reward. In the face of such dangers, the only safe course is to avoid all involvement with the false teachers. See Introduction to 1 John: Theology.

**7 gone out.** See note on 1 John 2:19.

**do not confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh.** The deceivers were Docetists, who denied the reality of the human nature of Christ (1 John 4:2 note). John’s wording of the confession that the deceivers reject—which could be rendered “Jesus as Christ coming in the flesh”—also refutes adoptionist views of Christ that drive a wedge between a human Jesus and a divine Spirit (Christ) that supposedly empowered Jesus temporarily. See theological note “The Humanity of Christ” on previous page.

**the antichrist.** See note on 1 John 2:18.

The apostles labored to instill in others faith in Jesus Christ who came in the flesh, through whom believers receive a full reward, eternal life, by God’s grace. Although some manuscripts read “you have worked” (cf. text note), the slightly better-attested reading indicates that John is referring to his own and other apostles’ gospel labors, as in 1 John 1:3, 4 (cf. Phil. 2:16).

verse_quote: Everyone who goes on ahead and does not abide in the teaching of Christ.
note: This refers to the false teaching of the Antichrist and his false teachers who seek to deceive. To be “progressive” and to “go ahead” in theological thought is not always good, as in this case. There is irony here, for a restless quest to move beyond the truth of the incarnation leads to a loss of the faith that the apostles labored to instill in others and, thus, to the loss of the “full reward” that belongs to believers in Christ (v. 8).

verse_quote: do not receive him into your house or give him any greeting.
note: This stern measure contrasts sharply with the exhortation given in 3 John 5–8 to welcome believers who proclaim the truth. Both epistles envision the first-century situation in which teachers traveled from town to town and were dependent for housing and board on the hospitality of those in the local Christian communities (cf. Luke 10:4–9; Acts 16:15). Such hospitality implied endorsement of a teacher’s ministry and message, so hosts needed to use theological discernment in offering their home as a “platform” for a visitor’s instruction (see Introduction: Date and Occasion). The prohibition here probably has to do also with the notion that continued close ecclesiastical fellowship with false teachers can infect a person; see, e.g., Paul’s statement that “a little leaven leavens the whole lump of dough” (1 Cor. 5:6), where an immoral person is to be disciplined by the church, and, if he is unrepentant, excommunicated, lest the immorality spread to others (cf. 1 Cor. 5:1–13). Consequently, here John says such continued intimate fellowship results in one’s “taking part in his [the false teacher’s] wicked works,” whereas Gaius and others who welcomed and aided traveling teachers of Christ’s truth became their “fellow workers for the truth” (3 John 8)., 11

A letter is no substitute for personal fellowship. John hopes to share with his readers the mutual encouragement that can only take place in person. He closes by bringing greetings from one Christian community to another, a common practice in apostolic letters and a reminder of Christian unity. “The elect sister” may refer to another church and her “children,” presumably members of that church. See note on v. 1., 13
